sections.history: Pennadam, the Pennagadam of the Tevaram hymns and also remembered as Thoongaanai Maadam, lies in the Nadu Nadu country of Cuddalore district. It is praised in the hymns of Appar, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The lord is worshipped as Sudarkozhundeesar, Pralayakaleswarar and Pushpavaneswarar, and the goddess as Kadanthai Nayaki, also called Aamodhanaambikai. A local reading of the town's name tells of maidens (penn), the divine cow Kamadhenu (aa) and an elephant (gadam) who all worshipped here, so that the place became Penn-aa-Gadam, later Pennadam. The main shrine is of the Early Chola period in style, and inscriptions attribute it to the legendary king Kocengannan, one of the seventy-eight temples credited to him; Chola and Vijayanagara inscriptions are also recorded.
sections.architecture: The sanctum of Sudarkozhundeesar is the temple's most distinctive feature: its vimana is shaped like the back of an elephant, the form called gajaprishta, and it is pierced by windows on three sides, a design that belongs to the Early Chola period. The Nandi is placed in an unusual position, turned toward the entrance and away from the sanctum, and temple tradition connects this with the legend of the flood. Beyond these features the sources say little of the towers and halls, so the account here stays with what is recorded.
sections.legends: The temple's great legend is of the deluge. When a primordial flood threatened the land, the gods turned to Shiva to protect all living beings. He commanded his bull Nandi to guard the place, and Nandi turned toward the entrance and drew in the rising waters, so that the town and its shrine were saved. From this the Lord is revered as Pralayakaleswarar, the Lord of the end of the age. A second tradition belongs to Appar. After he had sung a hymn of repentance for his years among the Jains, a divine messenger is said to have appeared and marked his shoulders with the trident and the bull, the signs of a Shaiva servant. The temple keeps both memories: a protector against the waters, and a Lord who receives the returning devotee.
sections.festivals: The sources consulted give no firm festival calendar for Pennadam, so this account names only the observances common to every Shiva temple: Maha Shivaratri in February or March and the monthly Pradosham. Local festivals, if any, follow the Tamil calendar; confirm dates with the temple.
sections.experience: Come to Pennadam to see the sanctum from outside as well as within: look up at the elephant-back form of the vimana and at the windows set into its three sides, then notice the Nandi turned toward the entrance, and recall the flood it is said to have drawn in. Worship Sudarkozhundeesar in the sanctum and Kadanthai Nayaki in her own shrine. The town is a quiet one beside the road to Virudhachalam, and many visitors link the temple with the story of Appar's return to Shiva.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Pennadam lies about 18 km south-west of Virudhachalam on the Virudhachalam–Tittagudi road, in Cuddalore district, and has a railway station of its own. Buses run along the road from Virudhachalam and Tittagudi. The temple stands in the town; confirm local transport on the day.
